en_summary: $JPM CEO Jamie Dimon says valuing a company is humbling: take an annual report, rip out the stock price pages, and estimate what it is worth. He notes people are often shocked by how wrong they are, as valuation is intellectually challenging.
text:
$JPM CEO Jamie Dimon: "You want to try something humbling? People think they’re very smart. Take home an annual report, rip out the pages that show the stock price, and then say what you think it’s worth.

It’s humbling how you value something, and it’s intellectually challenging."

text:
Non-asset owners are seeing a large drop in US consumer sentiment.

Since January 2026, consumer sentiment is down -27% among the bottom 33% of stockholders, the largest decline among the stock-wealth groups surveyed.

This is followed by those who do not own stocks, whose sentiment is down -25% over the same period.

By comparison, sentiment is down just -9% among the middle 33% and -7% among the top 33% of stockholders.

Asset ownership has helped offset the impact of higher living costs, leaving consumers with fewer or no stocks more exposed to the recent acceleration in inflation.

Meanwhile, 1-year consumer inflation expectations rose +0.1 percentage point this month, to 4.7%, its 2nd-highest reading since August 2025.

Own assets or be left behind.

name: Jason Furman
zh_summary: @jasonfurman談曼谷世銀與IMF年會：言辭一片悲觀但數據都正面，IMF上調預測，且已無人再關心關稅。
en_summary: @jasonfurman on the Bank Fund meetings in Bangkok: the words are all negative but the numbers positive, with the IMF upgrading its forecast, and no one cares about tariffs anymore.
text:
Some impressions from the Bank-Fund meetings in Bangkok:

1. The words are all negative but the numbers are all positive. Is all about unprecedented waves of shocks and risks while the IMF upgraded the forecast to something even stronger.

2. No one cares about tariffs anymore, they expect them to continue forever and have adjusted and moved on.

3. Everyone cares a lot about high interest rates. They expect them to continue forever but they haven't moved on.

4. Oil prices fall somewhere between these two. Everyone cares some, aren't sure if they'll continue and have partially moved on.

5. Everyone is having exactly the same conversations about AI as they are having here: will the demand boost continue, is it a bubble, will it kill jobs, when will it show up in productivity. I sensed much more optimism than pessimism and finance ministers and central bankers are not particuarly interested in p(doom).

6. No one seemed to mind that Scott Bessent didn't bother to attend.

Trying out the new Meta glasses from Thailand. Today’s topic is the Tesla flying car. I look at it from multiple perspectives. From just permitting, there’s a lot of challenges. What’s so interesting about it, the technology itself is getting there and I think for metropolitan areas it’s gonna be very difficult. For long-haul traffic it could be very cool. Or in rural areas, even better, flying around in your car. I love the idea. 

From a perspective of investing, here’s what I think is going to happen. I think there’s no question that Tesla’s going to merge with SpaceX because that technology is coming together like this. So if you own Tesla stock, you’re going to own New Co. If you already own SpaceX, hang in. You’re going to own Tesla. It’s going to happen that way. #shotonmeta #metaglasses

en_summary: Ledn co-founder Mauricio Di Bartolomeo calls rising borrowing costs a rounding error next to $BTC's upside, noting even the smallest Ledn loans (starting at 9.25%, smallest 11.49%) are cheaper than Strategy's 12% preferreds. He says anyone who borrowed at 9.25% when Bitcoin was 65-70 has seen collateral rise 25-35%.
text:
Ledn co-founder Mauricio Di Bartolomeo calls rising borrowing costs a rounding error next to $BTC's upside, with even the smallest Ledn loans cheaper than Strategy's 12% preferreds

"The cost of borrowing against your stocks just went up by 25 bps. How much are stocks up by this year?"

"The increase of the debt of the carrying costs has become a rounding error compared to the upside of the underlying position that loan is financing. It's similar to the dynamic we see with Bitcoin-backed loans."

"A Bitcoin-backed loan interest rate at Ledn starts at 9.25%. Anybody that took a loan from Ledn at 9.25% when Bitcoin was at 65 or 70 has seen the value of that collateral increase by 25 to 35%."

"As long as the cost of financing the debt is a fraction of the price action of the asset that debt is financing, we're still very much in the clear in terms of those ratios and that dynamic."

"Every single person at Ledn today, even at a $500 loan, can borrow at lower interest than what Strategy's paying on their preferreds. The smallest loan at Ledn is 11.49%. STRC yields are at 12% right now."

"There's no way we were gonna solve the deficit from within the government. The only way we're going to solve the national debt is with AI and robots. We're not gonna solve it by trying to save our way there. The appetite to cut spending is not there at the presidency, the House, the Senate or the judiciary. Basically, no one in authority in the government whatsoever — with maybe a few rare exceptions.

Maybe if the president made that his primary goal, we could do that. If you try to solve the deficit and stop wasteful spending, you make a lot of enemies. President Trump likes to be liked. He doesn't like people calling him, being upset about ... some funding being stopped. 

I kinda got carried away, basically and was gone for too long from my companies. What I should have done was be more in the background ... and probably only had it last for a month or two. I should have gone back and focused on AI a little sooner than I did."

The full podcast interview with Walter Isaacson drops this Tuesday.

The next four years are going to feel very different to anything we've lived through.

Your wages havent kept up with the cost of living for years now. That's the Everything Code. Governments have to keep debasing the currency to fund everything, and it's eating into your pay every single year. That part isnt new.

AI, robotics, energy, crypto... are moving so fast that the systems built for the old world cant keep up. Politics gets angrier and more divided. You cant trust what you see or hear anymore. Even the idea of running a business stops meaning what it means today. Nobody knows yet what it becomes.

This is The Economic Singularity, and The Exponential Age is pulling it towards us faster than anyone is ready for.

The window to get ahead of it all is closing.

It’s becoming clear that MMTers have a worse understanding of reserve accounting than we thought. 

What matters is the total remittances, not IORB in isolation. And yes, in recent years the Fed has been operating at a loss, which has been net stimulative relative to the large positive remittances of prior years even though this income effect was offset by the tighter credit conditions that accompanied the rate hikes, which were a clear net drag and help explain why inflation fell after 2022.

What’s even more off-base about the idea that this might cause inflation is that the remittances matter in rate of change, not just levels. Saying “there’s $500B of new income because of IORB” doesn’t mean we got inflation from it. If you got $100B every year for 5 years you don’t get ongoing inflation because the rate of change isn’t changing. And in recent years the net interest impact has been improving as the Fed’s annual losses have shrunk substantially, meaning the incremental addition to the consolidated government deficit from this channel has been getting smaller, not larger. They have the direction of the flow backwards and this exercise explains why their theory of inflation has been so wrong in recent years.
